GDPNow Tracking Slowdown in Q4

Consistent with my note yesterday morning, Q3 GDP came in at 3.37%, just 0.10 pt above the Atlanta Fed GDPNow’s final 3.27% nowcast, fitting both of the tendencies I (or I guess I should say Claude) flagged: 

1 - after a big drop in the final month, and 
2 - in third quarters, 

the actual print has usually come in close to but above GDPNow’s last read.

GDPNow has now landed within about a tenth of the actual print in 5 of the last 9 quarters.

Turning to Q4, the Atlanta Fed has now started tracking at 3.22%:

▪ Consumption +1.79 pts (vs +2.55 in the final Q3 nowcast)
▪ Business spending +1.22 (vs +1.73)
▪ Inventories +0.59 (vs +1.64)
▪ Government +0.21 (vs +0.44)
▪ Residential −0.18 (vs −0.13)
▪ Net exports −0.41 (vs −2.95)

My usual caveat: GDPNow’s early nowcasts of a quarter have historically run high. It has started above the advance print in 34 of 57 quarters (ex-2020), by 0.40 pt on average. All three 2026 openings ended well lower:
▪ Q1: 3.13% → 1.99%
▪ Q2: 3.70% → 1.50%
GDPNow Tracking Slowdown in Q4 Q3: 4.95% → 3.37%

Several posts in @C_Barraud’s morning brief flagged the return of Europe’s gas squeeze, a situation in large part of the continent’s own making.

Dutch TTF futures broke €100/MWh Wednesday for the first time since December 2022 (Bloomberg), more than triple the pre-Iran-war level. That leaves the EU in an uncomfortable spot after it failed to take advantage of a dip in prices this spring.

EU storage exited last winter at ~28% in early April vs. 35% a year earlier (European Gas Hub). Yet even as TTF fell to about $15/MMBtu (~€45/MWh) after the April 8 U.S.-Iran ceasefire, refilling lagged. The seasonal curve was inverted (winter contracts priced below summer), so expectations were for cheaper future prices, and the EU has no common mechanism to force injections. Spring injections ran ~20% below 2025.

Exacerbating matters, Brussels had loosened the rules in 2025, letting states fall up to 10 points short of the 90% winter start storage target under “difficult conditions” such as low seasonal spreads or high prices.

The result: EU storage is 74.6% full, ~15 points below the five-year average (Gas Infrastructure Europe). Equinor’s CEO says that’s the lowest for this time of year since 2011.

Adding to the pressure, a “Dunkelflaute” (a cold, windless, cloudy spell) is expected to keep German wind generation below 7 GW through next week, less than half this year’s average (Bloomberg).

The upshot? German day-ahead power for Thursday cleared above €300/MWh, about double October’s average (Epex Spot via Bloomberg). It was €13 on Sunday.

Energy Aspects warns TTF could top €200 if the winter turns cold and supplies stay tight, vs. a U.S. equivalent near €8.5. Europe let the forward curve, not policy, decide whether to refill, and now it’s bidding against Asia for spot LNG at more than twice the spring price.

American Association of Individual Investors (AAII) retail focused weekly investor survey edges less bearish:

AAII Bulls (those who see higher stock prices in 6 mths, blue line) edged up to 37.8% from 36.9% the prior week, moving back above the long-term historic average of 37.5% after a week below.

Bulls though remained below the level of the Bears (who see lower stock prices in 6 mths, red line), even as the Bears fell to 41.4%, the least in three weeks, from 45.8% the prior week (and further below the 53.3% six weeks ago, the highest since May 2025). 

That leaves Bulls above Bears just twice in the last 15 weeks. Bears also remain above the long-term average of 31.0% for a 37th straight week (and they’ve only been below it 9 weeks since Dec 12, 2024).

The Neutral camp (yellow line) rose to 20.7%, the most in three weeks, from 17.3% (which was the least since early April). It remains under the long-run average of 31.5% and has been over that only twice since July 2024.
